clue.text: Where, in Rugby, Tom Brown was embarking on a game?

definitions.text: Where, in Rugby, Tom Brown was

blocks.note: boarding a ship or train is embarking on it
house, or housey-housey, is an old name for the game of bingo

explanation.surface: A question about where the schoolboy hero of Tom Brown's School Days set off on some sporting contest at Rugby.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Brown's School Days is set at Rugby School, a fee-paying school where Tom lives in School House. 'Embarking on a game' reads like starting a match, but splits into two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Pupils at a residential school live in such a building, and Tom lived in one during his schooldays at Rugby.

clue.text: One scientist carrying damaged crate for another

indicators.note: something damaged is knocked out of shape, so the letters of the next word are rearranged
one thing carrying another holds it within, so the first scientist wraps around the reworked letters

blocks.note: a biologist is one kind of scientist
the five letters of crate rearranged

explanation.surface: One researcher hauls a broken wooden box on behalf of a colleague.
explanation.walkthrough: The reworked box letters go in right after the first letter of the scientist, not around the whole word or at its end.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue has already named one scientist, so 'another' stands for a second one: a specialist who studies germs and microbes.

clue.text: Fruit, or a sort of grain

blocks.note: taken as written
corn is a cereal grain such as wheat or maize

explanation.surface: A botanical question about whether something counts as a fruit or a cereal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' sets up a choice between two foods, but the clue simply says the fruit can be written as 'a' plus a grain.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanically the oak's nut is a fruit, the seed-bearing structure the tree produces.

clue.text: A rum business, perhaps, operating this manufactory

definitions.text: A rum business, perhaps, operating this manufactory

blocks.note: surface reading: an odd, suspicious line of work

blocks.clueFragment: A rum business, perhaps, operating this manufactory
blocks.note: setter's reading: a firm that makes rum and the spirits plant where it does so

explanation.surface: A shady or peculiar company running some factory.
explanation.walkthrough: Rum is British slang for odd or dodgy, so 'a rum business' sounds like something fishy; here it is literally a company producing the spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirits like rum, whisky and gin are made by heating fermented liquor in stills, inside a works built for that purpose.

clue.text: One in lower case? Not at all

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so the single letter goes within the next word

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
nether means lower; 'case' is the outside that holds the one

explanation.surface: A typographer wonders whether a character is a small letter, and is told no.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lower case' reads as small letters, but lower is the outer word and case says it encloses the numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as in 'me neither', the word adds a negative to a previous one, meaning not either and so in no way.

clue.text: Crown sick Tongan leader during dance

indicators.note: the leader is the one at the front, so only the opening letter of the islander is kept
something happening during an event falls within it, so these letters go inside the dance

blocks.note: a hop is an informal dance
ill means sick
the first letter of Tongan

explanation.surface: A Pacific king feels unwell in the middle of a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crown sick Tongan leader' reads as a royal phrase, since Tonga is a monarchy; crown is the definition, the summit of a rise.
explanation.definitionFit: The crown of a hill is its highest point, the summit at the top of the slope.

clue.text: Unsightly, or wanting in universal splendour

indicators.note: something wanting in a quality lacks it, so that word is taken out of what follows

blocks.note: U is the film certificate for universal viewing
glory means splendour
the little word of the surface is the part to lose

explanation.surface: Something is ugly, or else it simply lacks the splendour everyone sees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like a link offering a choice, but it is the letters taken out of the splendour word.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something unpleasant to look at, plain synonyms for lacking visual beauty.

clue.text: Praising old customs in Gateshead

blocks.note: ex- means former, old
a toll is a charge or duty levied, like a customs payment
taken as written
read as 'Gate's head', the first letter of the town name

explanation.surface: Someone sings the praises of traditional ways on Tyneside.
explanation.walkthrough: Gateshead is a town in north-east England, so it looks whole; the clue splits it as 'Gates head', the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To extol is to praise highly, so the present participle matches 'praising' word for word.

clue.text: Game southern girl outside Sussex resort taking drink?

indicators.note: the girl stands outside the rest, at the far end, after the resort and its drink

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for southern
Hove is a seaside town next to Brighton in Sussex
a half is a half-pint of beer
Penny is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A woman from the south waits outside a seaside town's pub, having a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Hove is a Sussex seaside town; a half is a British pub measure of beer.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a traditional British pub game in which coins are pushed along a marked board.

clue.text: Flighty type out of humour with Sikes, perhaps

blocks.note: out of humour means bad-tempered, cross
Bill Sikes is the villain of Oliver Twist; 'perhaps' because he is one example of the name

explanation.surface: A capricious character in a bad mood with Dickens's thug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flighty' suggests a fickle person, but it means a creature that flies.
explanation.definitionFit: A finch with crossed mandibles is a bird, so playfully a type of creature that takes flight.

clue.text: Fastener air force cadets held in left hand

indicators.note: what is held in a hand sits within it, so these letters go inside the others

blocks.note: L is short for left
the Air Training Corps, the RAF's youth cadet organisation
H is short for hand

explanation.surface: Young RAF trainees grip some fastening in their left hands.
explanation.walkthrough: The Air Training Corps is the British air cadet movement; its initials sit between L and H.
explanation.definitionFit: A bar that drops into a catch to keep a door or gate shut is a simple fastening device.

clue.text: Boredom of English upper-class shown in rejection of pub

indicators.note: something rejected is turned back, so the pub word is written backwards
shown in means displayed inside, so the class letter goes within the pub word

blocks.note: E is short for English
an inn is a pub
U means upper-class in British usage

explanation.surface: Posh English people are so jaded they turn their noses up at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from Nancy Mitford's 'U and non-U' usage. The pub word turns round to NNI before the U goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: The French loanword names listless weariness from lack of interest, which is the same feeling as boredom.

clue.text: Husband consumed with enmity

blocks.note: H is short for husband
consumed food means ate

explanation.surface: A married man is eaten up by hostility.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Consumed with' reads as eaten up by a feeling; 'with' is only the link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Intense hostility between people is the same as strong dislike, so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Bulgarian possibly appears to toil endlessly

indicators.note: endlessly means without an end, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: to slave is to toil

explanation.surface: A man from Bulgaria seems to labour without stopping.
explanation.definitionFit: Bulgarians speak a Slavonic language, so one is an example of that ethnic and language group, hence 'possibly'.

clue.text: Bathroom in south of France, or originally in Roman court

indicators.note: originally points to the origin of the word, its opening letter
one thing in another is placed inside it, so that letter goes into the court

blocks.note: sud is French for south
an atrium is the open central court of a Roman house
the first letter of or

explanation.surface: A bath in southern France, or one first built in a Roman courtyard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South of France' looks like a region, but it is the French word for south. The O goes after AT in the court.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweating room in a Roman bath house, used to work up a sweat like a sauna, is a bathing chamber.

clue.text: Blinkered Iberian writer given the chop

indicators.note: something given the chop is cut out, so the writer is removed

blocks.note: Spain and Portugal make up the Iberian Peninsula
a pen is a writing instrument

explanation.surface: A narrow-minded Spanish or Portuguese author gets sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iberian writer' looks like one author, but splits: Iberian is the adjective for the peninsula, the writer is what to cut from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with blinkers sees only straight ahead, so is narrow in outlook, like an island cut off from others.

clue.text: When at sea, curses tea clippers

indicators.note: at sea means confused and all over the place, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the nine letters taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Sailors swear about the tea aboard the fast sailing ships.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tea clippers' looks like the famous fast cargo ships; clippers here means garden shears.
explanation.definitionFit: Pruning shears used by gardeners cut through stems, so they are tools for clipping plants.

clue.text: Very proper girl — and a good-looking one

blocks.note: Pru is a girl's name, short for Prudence
a dish is slang for an attractive person

explanation.surface: A prim young woman who is also very attractive.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone excessively concerned with propriety and easily shocked is strait-laced and prim.

clue.text: With a lot of good fortune a bird finds food

indicators.note: a lot of means most but not all, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: luck is good fortune
the erne is the sea eagle

explanation.surface: A lucky bird manages to find something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: The erne, or sea eagle, is a crossword regular.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfalfa, also called lucerne in Britain, is grown as fodder for livestock, so it is animal feed.

clue.text: One-time politician in the grip of drink, for instance

indicators.note: something in the grip of another is held within it, so the politician goes inside

blocks.note: ex- means former, one-time
ale is beer
a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A former MP who has fallen prey to the bottle, to take one case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One-time politician' looks like a single unit to bury inside the drink, but only the politician goes in; the one-time part stays in front.
explanation.definitionFit: 'For instance' introduces a single illustrative case, which is what an illustration of a general point is.

clue.text: Church body rejected member backing this doctrine

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the church word is written backwards
backing means going in reverse, so the member word also runs backwards

blocks.note: the nave is the main body of a church
a leg is a limb, or member

explanation.surface: A church congregation spurns a member who supports this teaching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Church body' sounds like a synod or congregation, but it is the architectural body of the building.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the gospel, the good news preached by Christians, hence a body of religious teaching.

clue.text: Box under bottom of blade to catch the grass

indicators.note: the bottom of a word written downwards is its final letter, so only that one is kept
to catch something is to hold it, so these letters go around the box word

blocks.note: the last letter of blade
to spar is to box
taken as written

explanation.surface: A box placed beneath a blade traps some grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blade' and 'grass' make the surface a lawn, but the blade only gives its last letter. 'Under' is a placing word: the box sits under the E in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A tough Spanish and North African grass, this is used for making rope, paper and baskets.

clue.text: Spectators' manner of walking, say

indicators.note: say means as spoken, so the word wanted is one heard rather than spelt

blocks.note: a gait is a way of walking

explanation.surface: A comment on how a crowd of onlookers walks.
explanation.walkthrough: In British sport the gate is the number of spectators at a match, or the money they pay.
explanation.definitionFit: The attendance at a sporting event is called the gate, since the crowd comes through the turnstiles.

clue.text: Insect observed round apple core

indicators.note: round means turned about, so the verb is written backwards
the core is the centre of the fruit, so the middle letter is kept

blocks.note: saw means observed
the middle letter of apple

explanation.surface: A bug spotted crawling around the middle of an apple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Observed round' could be a single phrase, but round turns the verb backwards before the middle of the fruit joins it.
explanation.definitionFit: This striped stinging creature is a common flying insect, often found near fallen fruit.

clue.text: Deck officer's starting game before work

indicators.note: the starting letter is the first, so only that one of the officer is kept

blocks.note: the first letter of officer's
RL is Rugby League
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A ship's officer begins with a game before getting down to work.
explanation.walkthrough: Rugby League, RL, is a form of rugby played mainly in northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: The lowest deck of a wooden sailing ship, below the waterline, had this name.

clue.text: In Paris of Madagascar, the weird climbing mammal appears

indicators.note: climbing goes upward, and in a down answer that means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: the French for 'the', as signalled by 'In Paris'
rum is British slang for weird

explanation.surface: Somewhere in Madagascar a strange tree-climbing creature turns up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Paris' tells you to put the following word into French. 'Of Madagascar' tells the solver which mammal, since lemurs live only there.
explanation.definitionFit: This primate with a long tail, found only on Madagascar, is a furry tree-dwelling mammal.

clue.text: State cut prompts expression of concern

indicators.note: something cut is made shorter, so the end of the state is removed

blocks.note: Alaska is a US state

explanation.surface: A budget cut by the state sparks worries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State cut' sounds like government spending cuts; the state is a US one, losing its last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: This interjection voices sorrow, regret or worry, so it is an exclamation of distress.

clue.text: Sounds like Yorick's remains found in the boat-house

indicators.note: sounds like says the word is matched by its pronunciation, not its spelling

blocks.note: Hamlet holds the skull of the jester Yorick

explanation.surface: Hamlet's dead jester's bones turn up in a rowing club's shed.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hamlet, the gravedigger unearths the skull of Yorick, the late court jester.
explanation.definitionFit: A light oar or a small rowing boat is stored in a building where rowers keep their craft.

clue.text: Tree's single decoration is in character

indicators.note: something that is in another sits inside it, so these letters go within the character

blocks.note: a character in a story is a person
I is the Roman numeral one
the Military Medal, a British award for gallantry

explanation.surface: A tree's lone ornament matches its nature.
explanation.walkthrough: The MM, or Military Medal, is a British gallantry award. The 's stands for 'is', linking the tree to its wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a fruit tree producing orange, tomato-like fruit, also called the date plum or sharon fruit.

clue.text: Charity Pecksniff, member of a suitable order?

blocks.note: first meaning: in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit, Charity and Mercy are Pecksniff's two daughters
second meaning: a nun in a religious order devoted to charitable work

explanation.walkthrough: Charity is both a name and a virtue; as a name she is the sibling of another girl named Mercy, and as a virtue she fits a nursing order of nuns.
explanation.definitionFit: Charity Pecksniff's sibling is called Mercy, and a nun in that order fittingly practises charity, so one phrase serves both.
